title: SIU probing police chase, crash
article: A spokesman for Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) was saying little Thursday afternoon about the agency's probe of a provincial police vehicle chase that has left a Kingston man in serious condition in hospital.

The man, a 48-year-old whose name has not been released, remains in Kingston General Hospital where he is being treated for a broken leg and "possible" broken jaw, according to the SIU's Monica Hudon.
He suffered the injuries when his westbound sports car left County Road 2 west of Brockville and rolled into the ditch while being pursued by an Ontario Provincial Police cruiser.
The crash happened between Sherwood Springs Road and Yonge Mills Road shortly after 8 p.m. Wednesday and the stretch of road remained closed for much of yesterday.
"At this point, it's too early to say anything. It's still under investigation," said Hudon when asked about the status of the SIU investigation.
She said the speed reached during the pursuit as well as the officer's reasons for initiating and continuing with the chase will be part of the investigation.

Hudon could not say how many so-called subject and witness officers have been identified by the SIU. By law, witness officers are required to co-operate with the SIU, while subject officers have the right not to speak to investigators.

Provincial police spokesman Sergeant Kristine Rae said any information about the incident must come through the SIU. The Special Investigation Unit investigates cases where police interaction with the public results in injury or death.
Rae said police won't release the injured man's name unless he is charged, something she didn't expect would happen until early next week.

What police and the SIU have said about the incident is that it began when an officer attempted to stop the westbound sports car on County Road 2 near Yonge Mills Road for an unspecified traffic violation.
Rae would not say yesterday what violation prompted the pursuit, noting that was part of both the separate criminal and SIU investigations.

OPP said the marked police vehicle's lights were activated during the chase, but the driver did not stop. Shortly after the pursuit started, according to police, the Kingston man's vehicle rolled into the ditch.
The driver was initially taken to Brockville General Hospital, but was later transferred to Kingston General Hospital where he remained Thursday.
Wednesday night's incident comes as the SIU continues its probe of an OPP pursuit in July that ended with an Ottawa-area man being shot and killed.

Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau, 35, was shot by police near Forthton after OPP said he struck an officer with the pickup truck he was driving. Police say Charbonneau had fled a RIDE program set up on a Highway 401 off ramp in Brockville, setting off a chase along County Road 29.
Hudon had no new details on the SIU investigation into that case yesterday, noting the agency is waiting for the post-mortem examination report and results from the Centre of Forensic Sciences.
She would not speculate on a timeline to complete the probe.
"The investigations take as long as they take to make sure it's thorough and unbiased and impartial," said Hudon.
And over the Labour Day weekend this month, a police chase in Grenville County ended near Domville with several shots fired by police after they said a suspect attempted to run down an officer.
The SIU is not investigating that incident as the suspect was not injured.
Thomas Glen Shields, 32, of Edwardsburgh-Cardinal Township faces an attempted murder charge in the Sept. 6 incident that police say began with an investigation into a stolen vehicle.
Rae said police treat each pursuit separately when reviewing them, noting the circumstances differ in each case.
She said the decision to initiate a pursuit and continue with it is made by "individual officers and those who are monitoring the situation at the time."
"Each one is different because each situation is different - you can't just label them all the same," said Rae, who noted police chases are not an uncommon occurrence in Ontario.
"The fact that there have been incidents in this specific area, that's not under the officers' control," she maintained.

Earlier in the interview, Rae pointed out, "The fact that someone is fleeing the police, the onus is on the suspect - it's mandatory that those people stop when a police officer attempts to stop them.
"The fact that they are fleeing at that point, that part is duly on the suspect."
